name: Question 2
problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/00da8cdff7814df7368ff00924360db24a93934c5ae1c87ceb5daa6b00df37a7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}.
$$

Question 2
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is x2+3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
ddx(2v2)=−x2+3
b
ddx(12v2)=−x2+3
c
ddx(12v2)=x2+3
d
dvdx=x2+3
e
dvdx=−x2+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is x2+3 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−x2+3.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=−x2+3.

Now, since v=dxdt, we have vdvdx=−x2+3.(∗)

Finally, using the fact that ddx(v2)=2vdvdx⟹ddx(12v2)=vdvdx,

we can write our differential equation (∗) as ddx(12v2)=−x2+3.
